title: Caribbean Internet Café
protagonist: David Grant, MBA graduate and aspiring entrepreneur
primary_metric: CIC's expected monthly pre-tax operating cash flow, in Jamaican dollars, under the market research firm's REALISTIC demand scenario (40% of the 20,000-person target segment visiting an average of 3 times per year), before any split of profit between David and JTL

options.B: Accept and proceed with the CIC offer from JTL

legacy_conversion_note: This is a formalization of a REAL, professionally published business teaching case -- Ivey Publishing / Richard Ivey School of Business case 998B02, 'Caribbean Internet Café,' authored by Michelle Theobalds under the supervision of Professor Murray Bryant, copyright 1998 Ivey Management Services (the file on hand is Version A, dated 2009-09-09; product page confirmed live at store.hbr.org, see sources[] S1). Unlike A Coach's Dilemma (fiction), this case's protagonist, company, financing offer, market-research figures, and all Appendix B-E data are the real historical case-study record, not invented. The legacy source folder (source/Y2/Session 7/Caribbean Internet Cafe/) contains three files: the case docx (transcribed from, and cross-verified word-for-word against, the embedded original Ivey PDF -- confirmed byte-consistent, including footnote 1's exchange-rate figure), a 12-page 'Untitled document.docx' which is the house discussion-guide framework (kept and migrated into FACILITATOR.md's anchor ladder -- see FACILITATOR.md's header), and the original 5-page Ivey PDF itself. WHAT WAS CHANGED FROM THE LEGACY DOCX: (1) Challenge sections 1/2/4/5 were replaced with the current pipeline's locked boilerplate (doctrine/CHALLENGE_BOILERPLATE.md) -- the legacy docx used older, non-conforming wording for these sections; only Challenge 3's deliverables are newly authored, replacing the legacy's flat 'Appendix A, 11 questions' format with 5 concrete, math-forcing artifacts (D1-D5). (2) The original case gives NO independent loan-rate quote for a self-financed Option A -- this conversion adds Appendix F/MA1, a stated Modeling Assumption (NOT invented data) that models Option A's financing at the 25% Jamaican mortgage rate the case ITSELF quotes elsewhere (Background, 'mortgage rates were currently very high (25 percent per annum)') as the going market rate at the time. This is the single quantity this T4 case requires a student to assume and defend, per SPEC.md Section 3. (3) The Twist (FACILITATOR.md) is newly authored -- the legacy discussion guide's own two twists ('the future arrives early,' 'JTL changes the deal') are preserved in spirit and combined into one fully quantified version, grounded in the real, well-documented historical decline of Internet cafés as home broadband spread (sources[] S3) plus arithmetic already implicit in the case's own numbers (how much capital each option actually raises vs. needs). WHAT IS KEPT VERBATIM: every dollar figure, percentage, and quantity in Appendices B, C, D (JTL's offer terms), and E (market research) is the original Ivey case's own real, published data -- reproduced, not re-derived or estimated.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The true rate an independent Jamaican lender would have quoted David in 1996 for this specific loan exists in principle but is not accessible now -- the real Ivey case (S1) never records it, only the unrelated 25% mortgage-rate figure quoted elsewhere in the same source document (Appendix D/Background). MA1 uses that real, cited figure as the closest public analogue, a documented good-faith estimate, not an invented number -- but a different real lender could plausibly have quoted David something else, which is exactly what this flex sweep surfaces at +50% (margin widens to 31.3%, breaching the 20% cap, though the winner never flips).

modeling_assumptions.text: Option A's (going-alone) financing rate is assumed, not quoted. JTL's 10% rate (Option B) is a real, quoted, concessionary offer. The case gives no equivalent independent-lender quote for Option A's funding gap, so this case models it at the case's own quoted 25% Jamaican mortgage rate (Background/Appendix D) as the going comparable rate at the time -- a real, cited figure applied by assumption, not an invented number. This is the case's single load-bearing, T4-required assumption (see sensitivity_model.py FLEX and case.json.balance.stability).

JTL's $60-per-computer-per-hour Internet usage charge is modeled as incurred exactly when a customer PAYS for computer time -- i.e., a customer who 'shares' a computer with a paying customer rides along on that already-billed computer-hour rather than triggering a second one. Appendix C states 40% of customers pay and the rest share or don't use a computer at all, but does not specify how the JTL usage charge applies to sharing; this is a real, stated simplification.

A calendar month is modeled as 52/12 weeks (about 4.33 weeks) when converting Appendix C's weekly staff-hour figure into a monthly labor cost, and when converting Appendix E's annual visit-rate scenarios into monthly visit counts. A real calendar has months of varying length; this is the standard average-week convention, not the only defensible one (see sensitivity_model.py FLEX).

Appendix C's staff-hours figure ('needs staff on hand for about 90 hours a week, an average of two employees on duty at a time') is read as already being total weekly labor-hours (90), not a coverage-hours figure to be multiplied by the average headcount (which would give 180). Both readings are grammatically defensible; the source case does not disambiguate. This case adopts the 90-total reading throughout D1-D4 and sensitivity_model.py's canonical PARAMS; the alternative (180) reading narrows but does not flip the primary-metric margin (14.0% -> ~17.2%, still under the SPEC Section 2 20% cap) -- found during Tier 2 P1 cold-solve, 2026-08-17, and confirmed via sensitivity_model.py's staff_hours_per_week FLEX dial.

deliverables.text: A startup investment (PSI) table for CIC: every Appendix B equipment line item converted from its US-dollar unit cost to a Jamaican-dollar total, plus every other up-front cost (legal/incorporation/licensing/decorating, pre-opening advertising, utility deposit), summed to a single total Primary Sunk Investment figure, rounded to the nearest thousand Jamaican dollars.

A monthly financing-cost table comparing Option A's and Option B's interest expense: Option B's cost of servicing JTL's loan at its stated concessionary rate, and Option A's cost of financing the same funding gap at the market rate given elsewhere in the case (Appendix D/F) -- each converted from an annual rate to a monthly dollar cost.

A monthly operating-cost and per-visit contribution-margin table: every fixed monthly cost CIC carries regardless of financing choice, plus the net revenue CIC keeps from a single one-hour customer visit once its own internet and food/drink costs are subtracted.

A break-even table: the number of customer visits per month CIC needs, under each financing option, to cover its combined fixed costs and interest expense -- compared against the monthly visit count implied by each of Appendix E's three market-research scenarios.
An original bar graph comparing Option A's and Option B's monthly break-even visit count against the three Appendix E scenario visit levels (optimistic, realistic, pessimistic).

balance.argument_a: Every dollar of CIC's profit is David's alone: on Appendix E's realistic scenario David's personal monthly take-home under Option A is CIC's full net cash flow, a higher JA$85,045.83 (derived.net_cash_flow_month_A_realistic_jad), with no partner, no vote-sharing, and no long-term dependency on JTL beyond the Internet link itself. The 25% assumed borrowing rate costs JA$22,354.17/month (derived.interest_month_A_jad) -- real and expensive, yet still a fixed, known cost. Applied against Option B's actual 50% ownership split, Option A's JA$85,045.83 is roughly 75% higher than the JA$48,491.67 David personally keeps under Option B (50% of derived.net_cash_flow_month_B_realistic_jad, JA$96,983.33) -- the single largest, most decisive number in this case on a pure personal-take-home basis.
balance.argument_b: Halving the effective interest rate on a much larger loan saves real money every month: JA$10,416.67/month (derived.interest_month_B_jad) versus Option A's JA$22,354.17, an JA$11,937.50/month saving to CIC as a company. That financing is already confirmed rather than requiring David to convince an unnamed lender to say yes at all, and JTL's combined JA$2,250,000 raised (derived.option_b_total_raised_jad) against a JA$1,573,000 need (derived.psi_total_jad) leaves CIC a real JA$677,000 working-capital cushion (derived.option_b_cushion_jad) -- versus Option A's JA$0 cushion (derived.option_a_cushion_jad), since Option A raises exactly its shortfall and no more. Argument B does not win on David's personal monthly take-home once the 50% split is applied (see argument_a) -- its real case rests on certainty of funding and survivability under a bad year, not on out-earning Option A month to month.
balance.margin_basis: The GRADED primary metric is CIC's expected monthly pre-tax operating cash flow under Appendix E's realistic scenario, computed identically for both options except for financing cost (D2) -- a company-level comparison, deliberately scoped BEFORE any split of profit between David and JTL, because that is the comparison D1-D4's deliverables actually build and because the source case never specifies a dividend/payout policy for JTL's 50% stake. Option B's much lower interest expense (JTL's 10% vs. the assumed 25% market rate for Option A, MA1) gives it a real, close, disclosed edge on this company-level metric once every fixed cost and every unit of contribution margin (D3) is worked through in full. See derived{} for the exact worked figures; not printed in case.md. A SEPARATE, materially different comparison -- David's own personal take-home after Option B's real 50% ownership split is applied -- is NOT the graded primary metric (see the Modeling-scope note in Background/Appendix D of case.md), but is real, computable from the case's own given data with no extra assumption, and swings the other way by a wide margin: see personal_take_home_note below.
balance.personal_take_home_note: Found during Tier 2 P2 both-sides-solve, 2026-08-17. Applying each option's stated ownership share (100% David under A; 50% David / 50% JTL under B, per Appendix D) to the same realistic-scenario net cash flow figures used for margin_pct gives David a personal monthly take-home of JA$85,045.83 under Option A versus JA$48,491.67 under Option B -- Option A ahead by approximately 75.4% ((85045.83-48491.67)/48491.67), the OPPOSITE side from the graded company-level metric and more than 3x the SPEC Section 2 20% cap. This is not a new assumption -- it uses only Appendix D's own stated 50% equity split and the same D2-D4 cost figures -- and is why the primary_metric is explicitly scoped to company-level cash flow (see margin_basis) rather than silently absorbed into a claim that Option B is close to as good for David personally as it is for CIC. FACILITATOR.md's Sensitivity note and Socratic question 6 make this explicit for discussion; case.md's Background flags the scope without stating the number, so students must do this arithmetic themselves rather than read it off the page.
balance.stability: PARTIALLY stable under a ±50% flex of the case's genuine FLEX assumptions (see sensitivity_model.py). Flexing weeks_per_month (Appendix F MA3, base 52/12) ±50% (to 2.1667 or 6.5 weeks/month) never flips the winner and never breaches the SPEC §2 20% cap: margin ranges from 12.9% to 15.5%. Flexing staff_hours_per_week (Appendix F MA4, base 90) ±50% (to 45 or 135 hours/week) never flips the winner and never breaches the cap: margin ranges from 12.9% to 15.4%; the discrete alternative reading of MA4 (180 hours/week) also stays under the cap at ~17.2%. Flexing market_loan_rate_annual (Appendix F MA1, base 25%) ±50% never flips the winner (Option B always wins on this metric across the entire realistic range checked) but DOES breach the 20% cap at the upper flex: at 12.5% the margin narrows to 0.79% (comfortably inside the cap); at 37.5% the margin widens to 31.3% (over the cap). The cap is crossed somewhere near market_loan_rate_annual ≈ 29.7% -- well within the ±50% sweep. This is a genuine, disclosed instability in the case's one load-bearing assumption, not a modeling bug: MA1 is explicitly an assumption (not cited data) precisely because the case gives no independent lender quote for Option A, and this sensitivity is the honest consequence of that gap. Per DOCTRINE_LEDGER.md MCS-26/MCS-41, disclosure is the required response, not elimination. Separately, and NOT a flex-instability in the SPEC §2 sense: the company-level metric's winner (B) reverses to A by a wide, non-marginal margin (~75%) once Option B's 50% ownership split is actually applied to David personally -- see personal_take_home_note above; this is not something a ±50% parameter sweep surfaces because it is not a sensitivity to an assumption, it is a different metric definition entirely.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from case.md's given (real, sourced) Appendix B-E data plus Appendix F's stated assumptions; case-readiness should re-derive independently, not just trust this block. See sensitivity_model.py for the runnable version of every figure below.

sensitivity_note: A business-financing case with no illness/death content requiring a SPEC.md Section 6 flag, though the personal stakes (risking life savings, giving up half a company) are real and worth naming gently. The primary metric's stability is only PARTIAL -- see balance.stability and FACILITATOR.md's sensitivity note before defending a specific margin number in discussion. Also see balance.personal_take_home_note: the graded company-level metric (margin 14.0%, B ahead) and David's own personal take-home once Option B's 50% split is applied (margin ~75.4%, A ahead) are two different, both-real metrics that point opposite directions -- a facilitator defending 'the margin' should be explicit about which one is meant.

cohort_bands.note: Anchors 1-4 run as written; the room typically reaches the interest-rate trap (D2 alone) before D3/D4's fuller cost picture narrows the gap -- expect real movement at both the D3/D4 reveal and the Twist.
Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; D1's equipment-conversion table is worked as a shared example for the first 5-6 line items before pairs finish the rest and D2-D4 independently.

No vote to take -- Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a physical move; guide plays devil's advocate directly, specifically defending the raw 10%-vs-25% interest-rate comparison to see if the Hero catches the trap (that it is only one piece of the monthly picture) unprompted.
